summary:
Caribbean Netherlands comprises Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law on civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination extends to the islands, and the statutory framework operating in the European Netherlands applies here in the same form.

That protection covers visitors as well as residents. Travel-facing coverage of the region treats Bonaire as a destination where strict anti-discrimination statutes stand behind an equality-friendly welcome, and the island markets itself on that basis.

Same-sex unions have been registrable since 4 December 2012, when the Census Office in Saba recorded the Caribbean Netherlands' first: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on the island; both were visiting, which establishes that the registry performs civil ceremonies for persons without island residency.

Ceremony logistics are documented on Saba. The Court Room in the Administrative Building is identified as the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony, the registrar of record is documented as flexible with couples' wishes, and full destination-wedding infrastructure including caterers, florists and accommodation operates on the island. Civil ceremonies therefore run routinely through the local registry.
tangentialFactors:
GayCities (14 December 2022, updated 1 September 2023) ranks Bonaire fifth on a list of marriage-equality destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America. The ranking is a publication's editorial framing rather than a legal finding; the legal proposition it rests on, statutory anti-discrimination protection by virtue of the territory's status within the Netherlands, is separately sourced.

The 2012 registration joined two foreign nationals, one Aruban and one Venezuelan, neither resident on the island. The civil registry is consequently used by transient international couples as well as by inhabitants, which is relevant to a visitor expecting to complete paperwork locally.
localsOnly:
Residents of the three islands conduct civil-status business through the local registry. On Saba, civil ceremonies are held in the Court Room in the Administrative Building, and the registrar of record is documented as flexible about couples' arrangements.

Inhabitants are covered by the Dutch anti-discrimination statutes, which apply on the islands in the same wording and with the same force as in the European Netherlands.

Destination-wedding services operate locally on Saba, so couples marrying there are not obliged to source caterers, florists or accommodation off-island.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition or amendment of sex markers on identity documents in the islands. Whether the Dutch procedures for marker amendment extend to these special municipalities unchanged, and what processing route a resident would use, is unresolved here.

The enforcement record of the anti-discrimination statutes is not sourced. No hate-crime enhancement, complaint outcome or prosecution is documented, and the inventory contains no reports of violence against trans people in the islands with dates or outcomes.

Entry and visa requirements, airport or port screening that could expose a traveller's trans status, bathroom and facilities rules, and access to gender-affirming healthcare are not covered by these sources.

Every source supplied concerns marriage registration, equality marketing or ceremony logistics. None is trans-specific, so any statement about what a trans visitor faces rests on the general extension of Dutch statutory law rather than on trans-specific evidence.
